prompt: NO₂ has 17 valence electrons in total. What does an odd count tell you before you draw anything?
choices: One electron must be left unpaired — it is a radical
The species must carry a charge
The structure must contain a triple bond
explanation: Nitrogen brings 5 and each oxygen brings 6, so 5 + 12 = 17. Electrons are used in pairs — bonding pairs and lone pairs — so an odd total guarantees one is left over with no partner. NO₂ is a radical, which is why it is brown, highly reactive, and a component of smog.
teach: Count total valence electrons before drawing. Odd → radical: one atom cannot reach an octet, and the species will be reactive and often dimerizes. Even → an ordinary Lewis structure should be reachable. This costs five seconds and tells you what kind of species you are dealing with.

prompt: NO₂ (17 valence electrons) dimerizes to colourless N₂O₄ when cooled, but nitrite, NO₂⁻ (18 valence electrons), does not dimerize. Why?
choices: NO₂'s unpaired electron pairs with another molecule's to form an N–N bond; NO₂⁻ has none to offer
NO₂⁻ already reaches an octet on every atom by forming two double bonds
Dimerization requires a positive charge, which NO₂⁻ lacks
NO₂⁻ is the more reactive of the two and decomposes instead
explanation: Adding one electron to NO₂ gives nitrite 18 — even, fully paired, nothing left over. NO₂'s spare electron is effectively half a bond looking for a partner, and two of them make the N–N bond of N₂O₄. That bond is weak, so warming the gas breaks it again and the brown colour returns.
teach: Pairing two unpaired electrons IS a bond, which is why radicals dimerize on contact. The same fact drives radical chain reactions: a radical meeting a closed-shell molecule cannot simply pair off, so it makes a new radical instead and the chain continues.
